utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody, and welcome. Madam Usher -- Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ma'am. All the accused are present. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Krgovic and the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Ms. Condon. Mr. Meek, the reason I assume Mr. Stojanovic is busy working elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same place for Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Prosecution, I notice Mr. McCloskey; that's it. One against seven or times three. Good morning to you, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are going to proceed with your testimony this morning, but we are going to do so with the bench consisting of three Judges only. Judge Stole couldn't be with us today, and, therefore, we are in agreement sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis (a). Okay. How are you feeling this morning? Are you better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little worse than yesterday, but I'll manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We hope to bring your testimony to an end as soon as possible. Mr. Bourgon, you were still in possession. Please go ahead and try to conclude as quickly as you can, please. Avoid repetitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good Morning, Mr. Galic. Let me begin by going back to the forward command post Kitovnica operations duty log, and if I can have this on E-court, P347 [Realtime transcript read in error "437"], pages 49 in B/C/S and page 44 in English. And that's -- Mr. Galic, this is where we left off yesterday. My first question, which you can answer, is that you recognise the signature of Major Obrenovic, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Obrenovic, where he signs, he states and certifies that this notebook contains 100 pages. Now, I counted the pages, and they are less. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Neither did I form this notebook, nor did I certify it, nor did I count the pages. So I don't know. And 12 and more years later, I really can't say anything about something that I didn't do, even if I had done it. After so much time, I wouldn't be able to assert whether there were as many pages as is indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. For the sake of the transcript, the page we're referring to is ERN 00760316. That will be important for the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the 65 -- 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that's the e-court. I said P347.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 347. That should be corrected, line 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to go back now to the previous page, which is, in B/C/S, page 48, and then again to page 47. Is it possible to have the English version side by side? You notice, Mr. Galic, that the last three pages of this book are empty, which on the English side we can see because the ERN numbers are mentioned, where it says that page 0314 is blank, page 0315 is blank, and the statement by Mr. Obrenovic is on 0316. My question is simply: Can you explain why there are three empty pages at the end of this book?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know how I can explain it. Probably there was no duty being done, it was not filled, and on the last page is the certification of the notebook. If I understand the question, maybe there was no duty being done during that time, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. Let's go back to English, page 6, and B/C/S, page 8. And I draw your attention, Mr. Galic, to the entry which is for 14 July. You have it in your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can scroll up a bit so the 14 July is easier to see for Mr. Galic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The entry for the 14th, and the second paragraph, where it says: "Enemy forces are very active over the communication lines and are preparing to attack our forces." Do you see that, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And since you said that this was your writing, do you -- can you explain to us, what does this refer to, this paragraph? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: These are reports from units that were coming in on the basis of the situation in the field, and through the communication means they heard and understood that the enemy was preparing to attack the positions of our units. That is the gist of this entry in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right, Mr. Galic, in saying that whoever wrote this, that it was a person at the IKM, and the mention is that they could listen to the enemy forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Operations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when we talk about enemy forces, we're talking about the 2nd Corps or the column that was approaching; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: In this case, that they are 2nd Corps forces preparing to attack our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, do you know, Mr. Galic, who or what is Premier?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Now, let me see if I can remember. It is the code name for someone. Now, I can't remember offhand who it is. There were several such code names, so I can't remember exactly who this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I'll try and help you by saying that Premier is the person or persons who could -- who had the capability to intercept communications from the enemy. Does that help you out?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I didn't come across that, so I'm not familiar with these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because what I would like to suggest to you, Mr. Galic, is that the -- at the forward command post, Zvornik Brigade did not have any capability for listening to enemy forces, and I wonder where that information could come from, that second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I said that it was only from the units that this message could have come, and this was noted. If it had come from some other source, it would have to be conveyed to units, if the information came from some other source. So in my opinion, what is written here is what I've just said. I can't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. Let's move on to a different topic, Exhibit 3D118, which is a three-page document in English and in B/C/S. And just before this document comes up, Mr. Galic: Would you agree with me that the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade did not have any capability to listen in to the conversations of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but in that period everyone was listening in to everyone else, and everyone had the capability to intercept communications if they had the necessary equipment; not myself, but there were all kinds of listening in and information obtained in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know, Mr. Galic, that Premier -- I understand you told me you don't know that -- what Premier was, but I suggest to you that Premier would only report his or its information to the Zvornik Brigade command and not to the IKM. Is there anything you can comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I don't know that. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I ask you now, Mr. Galic, to look at the document which is before you, which is the first page of a statement you provided in Bijeljina on 28th of August, 2003. Do you recognise what is before you? And then we'll move on to the second and the third page so that you can see the date.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page, please, on both sides? And just on the right side, if we can move to the third page just so that we can see the date, and then we don't need to move the English, which also has the date. Do you recall, Mr. Galic, giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was on this date in the afternoon and the evening, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember the date as being 28 August 2003?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: To judge by this document, yes, that is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is this your handwriting, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can refer you back to page 2, so English we don't need to change, but just page 2. Now, this interview took place on 28 August 2003, which is after the second interview you had with the Prosecution. My question is: Is there a reason why you stated that you were on duty at the forward command post on the 14th of July, but you did not say anything about being on duty on the 13th of July or the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I said that I was on duty on the 14th. That's what I said. As for the rest --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. We will move on to a different topic, and that is the discussion you had with the lawyers of Major Obrenovic. And first I would like you to confirm, because it's not clear from the transcript of your response two days ago, and I quote the reference then was at page 73, lines 17 to 25, and line [sic] 74, lines 11 to 15. I asked you a question, and then the presiding Judge also asked you a question, but I'm not sure it was clear that you did meet with the lawyers of Obrenovic 1 to 1.5 months before your second interview with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I said that I had met with them at their request, but not in the way in which you describe those people had arrived. That was what I reacted to. It wasn't in the way you said. They simply came to see me, like any other normal people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in at this time, Mr. Galic, is not the manner but rather that it was one month to 1.5 months before your second interview, which is what you stated during the interview. I'm talking about the second interview with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that you asked me whether I had spoken to the Defence of Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, when was this, before or after your second interview with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I think it was before the second interview, but one should look at the documents and the dates. I can't remember the dates. There must be a record somewhere which we can look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There is indeed a record. I'm just asking you if you recall. And my second question is: Do you recall that when you were initially asked --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can have on the e-court, please, the second interview, which is document 3D116, and I would like to have B/C/S page 53 and English page 29. Side by side, if that is possible. In the English side, I refer the Trial Chamber to lines 23 and 24, where it states -- the question was asked to Mr. Galic -- the question was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have it before you, Mr. Galic, on the right side, where you have the question which was put to you -- the question was at line 23 -- I'm sorry, for the English version, it's page 29 and not 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it in English, and let's make sure that the witness has the B/C/S. I'm not quite sure whether he has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you see the question which was asked of you: "Have you spoken to any of the lawyers of the men detained in The Hague for the Srebrenica execution?" And your answer was: "No, although there are quite a few things that remain unclear to me." Can you see this in your language, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it was on the screen in the -- I have been trying using as a beacon the word "security." Yeah, okay, where I take it he can -- he can see it now, I suppose. Yeah. Now, it's -- you leave it where it is, it's one, two, three, four, five. The fifth paragraph from the top of the screen. The interpreter, [B/C/S spoken], et cetera. Can you see it now, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page, in the English also.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in this document, Mr. Galic, it says here whether you had -- the lawyers of Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic, "and they insisted on having a discussion with me and they spoke with me." And the question was: "When was this?" "I don't know the exact date, but it was a month or a month and a half ago."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be the previous page in B/C/S. It's here. Oh, thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At the top part, Mr. Galic, where it says -- or I can see it says: "I don't know the exact date. It was a month or a month and a half ago, and they insisted." Now, how did they insist in meeting you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: They asked, as I said, that -- they talked to me, since I was an officer in the brigade command, and they wanted to talk to me in connection with the defence of Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to the last part of my cross-examination and, Mr. President, I would like to go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private or closed? Private? Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, I just mentioned to you five names, and according to these people you were not at the forward command post when they were there. More specifically, according to one of them, Drago Nikolic was there at the forward command post all day on the 13th and until the 14th of July in the morning. My question is: Does that help you remember the events as they unfolded in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move to my next question, and I need to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go back to private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, according to this person, you actually had a meeting with this person to discuss what he had said concerning the presence of Drago Nikolic at the forward command post on the 13th and 14th. Do you recall having this conversation with (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I never discussed that question or other matters with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First you ask us to go into private session so that you keep his name, and then you mention his name yourself, so let's redact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My mistake, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay, it happens, but we waste time like that. So in -- on page 13, line 3, please, delete the name of the individual, and you don't need to delete anything else. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can go back into private session, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go back to private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galic, I mentioned the name of an individual, and according to this person, Drago Nikolic was picked up from the forward command post in the morning of 14 July in order to go to the Zvornik Brigade command. And according to this person, that person himself returned to the forward command post later that day. My question is: Does that help you remember the events of July 1995 as they unfolded?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question: During your testimony, reference was made to the fact that we met before, "we" being representatives or those representing Drago Nikolic. Can you confirm that this meeting took place in November of 2005?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The meeting, yes, but I do not remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that nothing much was discussed at that meeting because it was only a preliminary meeting; do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: We talked about a series of questions, you and your associates. There -- I don't have any written record of that conversation or interview, so I really don't know. I know that you were there, I know that we did discuss certain matters. I don't remember the exact date. That's all that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that for reasons unknown to us, you refused to meet us thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I did not refuse, but the lady who contacted me, I told her that I was travelling that day with my family to my wife's birthplace. I don't know if you remember that, but I do remember it. I would have talked at any other time that I was free with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Galic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. So now, Mr. Meek, yesterday you confirmed that you had no cross-examination. Is that -- is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZEROVIC
utterances.text: We have no cross-examination for the witness, as we indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can confirm that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's just you, Mr. Petrusic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Galic, I only have a few questions. I represent the Defence of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you if in the course of your duties at the Zvornik Brigade, you required the cooperation of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I had no need for cooperation. I, myself, didn't need that, because that would have been skipping over my two command levels in order to contact them. I didn't even have the opportunity to do that. I would have liked to go and meet the people there, but I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your communication ended at the level of the Drina Corps; could we put it like that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went up to the chief of the section for personnel affairs. I don't remember the exact name of the person, but it had to do with certain activities and tasks of that organ, if something was unclear, but everything else was done within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for personnel affairs, for organisation, mobilisation and personnel affairs in the Drina Corps was Colonel Jovicic [Realtime transcript read in error "Jovetic"], does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Colonel what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: He was on that duty first. After that, the post was occupied by Lieutenant-Colonel. He went to that establishment post from the Bratunac Brigade command, and he was the assistant commander for that section. At the moment, I cannot recall his name, but we had a lot of contacts during meetings, during briefings that we were invited to. I really cannot remember his name. Before him, it was Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means we need to correct line 21 in the transcript, because we have Colonel Jovetic, and it should be Colonel Jovicic, and the witness did mention his successor at least by his surname, but it doesn't show up in the transcript. Who succeeded Major Jovicic -- oh, not Major, Lieutenant Colonel Jovicic? Who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. If he cannot recall the name, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At this point, Witness, this is not so important, but I would like to put it to you that in July 1995, the assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation and personnel affairs in the Drina Corps was Colonel Radenko Jovicic, but as I said, at this point in time perhaps this is not so important.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak up?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to confirm the level at which you cooperated was the level of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, on the 2nd of July, 1995, the command of the Drina Corps issued an order that the Zvornik Brigade should allocate a brigade, the equivalent of a battalion -- a unit, the equivalent of a battalion, and send it to the Srebrenica region. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I know about that order, but according to the order I was not engaged or included in any activity pursuant to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you know about the order when it arrived at the command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know when it arrived, but I know about the order on the basis of which later tasks were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After the unit went into the field, into the Srebrenica region, did you receive any kind of instructions from your command or the Chief of Staff in order to replenish the unit of the Zvornik Brigade, since a considerable, elite part of it was going to a different front?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If it was necessary to mobilise personnel to a limited extent to replenish the ranks, who would issue such an order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The brigade command asked for permission from the Drina Corps command, and based on that approval and the order, the activity was carried out in relation to mobilisation of the reserve battalion and their further deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would the same procedure apply in the case of a general mobilisation in the Zvornik territory?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: As for the general mobilisation, I really cannot recall the legal provisions, but I think when we are talking about general mobilisation, a completely different procedure is employed in a particular municipality or in the entire republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We know, from the roster of attendance of senior officers, that you were absent on the 12th of July, the 12th, the 14th and the 15th of July. Was there a need then to engage certain materiel and equipment, and in that case, in the event of the absence of the commander, Colonel Pandurevic, would Dragan Obrenovic then issue an order to you or to your deputy to engage or provide this materiel and equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. If the commander was not there, then this task would be carried out by his deputy, as regulated by establishment and other regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We also know that on the 12th of July, there was a need to engage a certain number of vehicles at the level of your brigade and also at the level of the Zvornik Municipality. Did Dragan Obrenovic issue an order to utilise these vehicles at the level of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you could see that there is nothing mentioned anywhere which would indicate that these activities proceeded in the organisation and according to the order of the commander or the deputy of the Zvornik Brigade. This was ordered by completely different institutions and organs, so this does not apply to the Zvornik Brigade. Thus, the answer to your question would be, no, there were no activities or any orders undertaken by Mr. Obrenovic in that sense, referring to what you were just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So in order to utilise buses on the 12th of July, the order was issued by the Defence Ministry sector in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Please don't ask me about the documents I had in front of me yesterday, because now I would need to look at them again in order to confirm that. I confirmed yesterday that it was the -- a department of the Defence Ministry, I don't remember how many sections were mentioned, and this was also done by the Secretariat of the Defence Ministry. I'm just speaking off the top of my head. I cannot recall the specific information that I read out from the monitor yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Defence Ministry is a civilian organ?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have any further questions of this witness, but I thought it was an appropriate moment to deal with a small housekeeping matter before he faced re-examination. You'll recall that yesterday I asked him to look at a hard copy highlighted document, and after we had finished in court, we were in discussion with the court management about how best to use that as an exhibit, and it was decided that the best way to do it was to re-mark it with asterisks so that they would show up on the screen and then put it into e-court, and that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But the point is that in going through that process, we discovered that we had miscounted, and the figure I should have put to him was 23 dead, 20 on the 16th, and I thought it appropriate to raise it now lest he be cross -- or re-examined on the point that's our fault, not his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday I recall we're talking of the document which lists the dead in Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the transcript yesterday, we'll check it, you will find three on the 15th --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and 19 on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you want to correct that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Three on the 15th; 20 on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 20 on the 16th, okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, I understand you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe it should be hopefully very brief, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Keep in mind the state of health of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Galic. On the last topic of the -- the list, I won't spend much time on this, but the list of the -- the dead, if we were to look and give credit to the men that died on -- in that area during the 15th and 16th, would it be fair to include the areas not just of Baljkovica but of Parlog, Mevici Brezik, Crni Vrh, Kijici and Snagovo?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: People who were killed in that area in Baljkovica, Crni Vrh and the immediate vicinity, yes, but Kijici are not in the area of the Zvornik Municipality, I think that belongs to either Bratunac or Milici, to either of those municipalities, I'm not sure, but it's not in the -- or it's not part of the Zvornik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thanks for that correction. And are you aware of how many young Serbian MUP soldiers died in that time period in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the list that we saw of the dead include the missing?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No. The list of those killed that we looked at yesterday is just the list of those killed. It's not a list including the missing or the wounded, either likely or seriously wounded. It's just a list of those killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just the previous question of yours, "young Serbian MUP soldiers," who do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm referring to the special police brigade battalion that were there, the members of the CSB Zvorniks that were there. I -- it's something I have not looked into fully, but I know they were there and they were fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go briefly back to the duty officer notebook, and that has been numbered -- for 13 July, it's number 377, and it's on the B/C/S, it is 5743. It's page 125 of the B/C/S and page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the top of the page, I think we went over this briefly, and I'll read out the English, and it will be coming soon, but it says: "The 5th Infantry Battalion. Combat readiness raised to the highest level. Couriers have been dispatched in order to mobilise all men and send them to their units." Do you get involved in the mobilisation at that level or is that a different level from you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This is not a mobilisation of new men. People would stay in the unit for a specific period of time, seven days or fifteen days. They would be at the positions, and then after that they would spend a certain period of time at home, resting. So some people were at the position, some were at home, resting. So probably the commander of the 5th Battalion sent his courier to bring all the people who were resting back to the unit. So this is not a mobilisation of new personnel. The commands would work for themselves in accordance with a previously-established order or according to previously-issued orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. And can we go to a Defence exhibit, 7D99. This is a 14 July 1995 document, and could you just read it briefly again so we see the gist -- or we see what it's about, just the part that stops with "Za," just the three lines?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: "In order to secure the medical centre, Zvornik, carry out mobilisation of seven conscripts, the mobilisation is to be carried out immediately. Chief of the personnel affairs sector, Mihajlo Galic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can we go to the -- the stamp and signature? Again, I think you've dealt with this, but I wanted to -- I wanted to get a little more detail on you. We see the stamp, and it's covering up some -- some letters. Can you tell us what those letters are? It looks like a "PNN" and an "S" with a -- or "Sh."

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: "Sh."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It's a stamp of the military post.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: And then there is the typed signature, chief of the sector for personnel and replenishment, Major Mihajlo Galic, so this was not actually signed by me but somebody -- but by somebody else in my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- what does, and this will sound funny in the translation, but what does "Za PPP" mean?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The "P" stands for Pomocnik [phoen] "assist deputy," for deputy. Because at that -- actually, I was not there that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So sometimes when an officer is not there, his subordinates can sign for him by putting "Za" and then his name, like in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on the 14th of July, just tell us again where you were when your subordinates were doing this business?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was on duty at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to spend a little bit of time on this topic to try to see if we can clarify some of this. Is it a serious thing when you're told to go to the forward command post to take an unscheduled duty?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Each assignment that I carried out, including serious tasks, I took them very seriously. I did not distinguish between easier or more difficult tasks, but approached each one with the same amount of seriousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you be in serious trouble if you refused to follow that order to go to the IKM that night?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Indeed, I would be in serious trouble, and I would probably be called to task and -- for failure to observe discipline by the superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you'd gone to that post that night and left your post unauthorisedly, would you also be in serious trouble?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: If I didn't receive an appropriate order and I do that on my own accord, yes, I would be in very serious trouble and I would have to be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it ever appropriate to take the IKM logbook away from the IKM?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. Take it where? Could you clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't know, but take it away from the IKM back somewhere away from the IKM on the, let's say, the 14th and 15th of July, in the middle of very tense hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: That logbook could not be removed from that location because it couldn't even be taken to the observation tower. It was always at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that a book that the, for example, the commander or the deputy commander needs to rely on when he shows up there to determine what might have happened during the days that preceded him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: If there are certain entries which are important, it is up to the commander and the Chief of Staff to judge and to see what is of interest to them, what they wish to use and what they need for their work. So I don't know quite how to answer. Whatever he needs, he looks for and he familiarises himself with those entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would it be a serious offence to put false entries in that book?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I think that will be absolutely inappropriate, and it wouldn't serve anyone's interests. I don't see why anyone would put down something that was not true, something that he hadn't seen or experienced at that point in time at that location. I don't see why anyone would do that, myself or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you imagine Drago Nikolic putting up for one minute a false entry putting him at a place or giving him a duty that was not true?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Knowing Drago Nikolic as a highly-professional soldier and a responsible individual, I don't think he would ever put down something that wasn't true and that isn't a true and real fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would he let you get away with doing that, either, especially if it involved him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not, in view of the opinion I have of him and I have already said, that he was a real professional and he wouldn't get -- let anyone get away with such a thing, not just me but anyone else, to put down an untruth in a document that has some lasting value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me go to just a couple of documents on a topic that Mr. Petrusic had asked you about. The first one is a Drina Corps document; that is, 65 ter 871 that I just had in front of me. And if we could bring that up in both languages. But I will start -- well, there you can make out that small print. If we could get the -- the English, but I'll start to read a bit of the English while we're waiting. This is something on the date of 12 July from the command of the Drina Corps, from Commander Zivanovic on the 12th called "The Provision of Buses for Evacuation From Srebrenica Enclave," and it's an order to the Zvornik Brigade, among others. And you can take a look at it, but it -- it basically is asking for available buses and to be sent -- to procure them and to send them to Bratunac. Now, I think from the roster, you may not have been there on the 12th, but do you remember this -- this order coming in from the -- from the Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, nor do I remember, nor did I ever see this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to another one. It's the Zvornik Brigade document related to this, 12 July, 65 ter number 322, and if we could put both the B/C/S and the English on the -- on this. There's the B/C/S. If you could try to make out as best you can on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not very clear, Mr. McCloskey. I think instead of having a split scene -- split screen, why don't we concentrate on the Serbo-Croat one, and we can follow from our screens then the English version. It's still not very clear, and for someone who knows the language, it could be understandable, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Take your time and take a look at this. And when the English comes up on my screen, I'll ... Okay. This is a -- as you can see, it's a regular combat report to the Drina Corps from the Zvornik Brigade, which you talked about those reports a bit, and there's a note in it that says, in that second paragraph: "We sent to Bratunac, pursuant to your order, eight buses from Drinatrans, two buses from the military post and four of our trucks." Did you or your office get involved in that mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. I wasn't in the office that day, nor in command. I had a day off. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've talked quite a bit about the mobilisation process, but there's a process by which when the army needs something in an emergency or a combat situation, that they can get it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: That is right, in accordance with the procedure that I described yesterday. That is stipulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those buses that sent -- were sent to Bratunac, those didn't go through your office, those were procured in some manner, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Not through the department I worked in or the command of the Zvornik Brigade. None of that went through those institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we see the signature line on the bottom of this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he can see it on the screen as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, we need to switch to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's under the name of Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, and as you saw from paragraph 2, it said "we sent." So it's pretty clear the Zvornik Brigade had some involvement in -- in following the Drina Corps order that we had seen before; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you are right. I know that there was no participation. Now, whether someone ordered someone else to send so many buses, I don't know. As for the signature here, I don't see how anyone could have signed this when this man, the signatory, was not in Zvornik, according to the best of my recollection at the time. It's not logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you would have received an order from Vinko Pandurevic from Zepa, would you have followed it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: If I had received an order, Vinko Pandurevic had his deputy at the time who would stand in for him, and it would be logical for him to relay that order to me, and I would act upon it. I would have to do that because he was my superior officer. So I would have to carry out all assignments given to me by my superior, the Chief of Staff, or the commander. I would do it unless it was something that is prohibited by law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, those two letters in front of the name "Vinko Pandurevic," what are they, "MOMD"? What do they represent? I mean, the witness can perhaps help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you help the Court? We see the word "Commander," and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- "Lieutenant-Colonel." Can you tell us what the next Cyrillic letters mean? We also see "Vinko Pandurevic," but can you tell us what the two letters before that are for us --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: In front of in the first and last name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It is a title which Mr. Pandurevic had. He was a Master of Sociology, sociological sciences, MA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was there, and I didn't know whether it was some kind of another "Za," someone standing in for him, so I needed to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, and thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you got an order directly from Vinko Pandurevic from Zepa over the phone, would you have followed it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I would follow the order if the order was addressed to me and my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: These are all assumptions, of course. If he failed to get in touch with the Chief of Staff, who stands in for him, and if I was the operations officer on duty, he could tell me to do such-and-such, give me such an order. However, in that period of time, Vinko Pandurevic did not issue any orders to me, and all the activities that may have related to me linked to the replenishment of units and things like that were not addressed to me, and in that period of time I had no contact with him on any issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While he was away, was he still the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: If he's away, the corps command, I think that is their responsibility, would in writing order that the brigade commander should be represented by the Chief of Staff. I know this because there were several occasions when the commander was absent, and there were some orders that arrived and that reached me, others didn't, so the rule and the procedure is as I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that, but if Dragan Obrenovic is acting as deputy commander of the brigade in the absence of his commander, is the commander, Vinko Pandurevic, still in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, but that is my personal opinion, he's not the commander, he is replaced by his deputy who has all the authorisations of the commander, because if Mr. Pandurevic is engaged for a certain period of time or if this applies to any other commander, and if he's away, tens of kilometres away from the territory of Zvornik Municipality, it is only logical that in that period of time he would be replaced by his deputy. This also applies during leave, medical treatment, et cetera. As an example, I can say that in the absence of the Chief of Staff, the Deputy Chief of Staff replaces him on the basis of an appropriate order. I don't know whether I have managed to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we'll get in a debate about it, but I'll ask you one more question on it. Do you think you could be getting confused with the title of acting commander when the corps or the brigade commander actually designates the deputy commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to object. He's cross-examining his own witness here. I think the question is asked and answered. He should ask open questions to this man who he called as his own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Galic and I are having a perfectly reasonable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- exchange on a topic that was brought up. I don't see any problem or any need to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. McCloskey, but, please, you're very near the borderline, according to us, very near the borderline. As long as you seek a clarification from the witness, okay, go ahead, proceed, but please don't try to go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you distinguish, in military terms -- have you been trained on the difference between the deputy commander and the acting commander in the absence of a commander?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, not fully. What I am saying, I'm saying on the basis of my own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just another question or two on emergency mobilisations. If a battalion command post was overrun by the enemy, would you expect the Zvornik Brigade to have to go through some kind of a mobilisation process to take over a house to replace the overrun command post?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: With one's own forces, the situation would be regulated along the defence lines. It is quite logical that the command post will have to be relocated to a place that is more suited for the work of the people in the battalion command, so that they might successfully have control over all activities taking place along the line or region of defence assigned to that battalion. Therefore, if you're referring to the 4th Battalion, as far as I can remember, their command place was burned down and they were relocated. I wasn't there in the field, I don't know, but later I learnt that it was moved to another location, and it took time and resources for it to be fortified so as to be suitable for use for what it was intended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But my question is, in particular: Before the commander and his soldiers can go into that building and start using it as a command post, do they have to go through some mobilisation process in the middle of combat, or can they just go into that building and take it over and start operations?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. It's not a building. It can be a trench, a bunker made from logs, planks, et cetera, and the command does it with its own personnel without any kind of additional mobilisation. They do that. They provide shelter for themselves, to be able to seek shelter from any attack or climatic changes. They do that, themselves. Their own unit does it. No one else does it for them. If the need should arise for certain concrete or construction elements, then that is something else. Then if it is a trench or a container that can be secured, but it is adjusted to the needs of that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the need should arise at the same time for a shelter to put in prisoners, would the command, on its -- as you've described it, be able to do that as well without going through some sort of mobilisation process?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to clarify the question, because I'm not sure I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if in a situation the Zvornik Brigade takes prisoners in the field, can they take over a local house to put those prisoners in without going through some mobilisation process?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: In the field, whatever we used was mobilised. When the forward command post was being relocated, there was no mobilisation. I'm not aware of any kind of mobilisation, nor of any house being used, because there weren't any such houses in that area, especially as in the surroundings of the command post all the buildings had been destroyed and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what building or facility was used to replace the command post of the 4th Battalion after it was overrun?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The command post was not overrun, it was simply burned down, and it was relocated. I went there much later. I think it was some sort of a container, and then there were logs and trees used to build something. I really don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the school at Orahovac being used temporarily after the 4th Battalion command was burned down?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, nor was that facility mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not by you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, thank you very much for your patience and all your time. I don't have any further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, Mr. President, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the presence of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony and also wish you a safe journey back home. Before you leave this courtroom, however, I enjoin the Victims and Witnesses Unit to give the witness all the attention that he requires, medical and otherwise. Make sure that he is comfortable, pending his transfer to where he resides. Okay, thank you. And we'll have a break now of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness. We will -- before you start giving evidence, we need to process the filing of the tendering of documents from the previous witness. You don't need to follow because it doesn't concern you. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm in your hands as to whether we do that now, but I was just in discussion with your clerk, and I was going to set out, in a spreadsheet form, the documents I wish to tender, which I haven't done yet, I confess, and I wondered whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can postpone it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- we can postpone it, and then it will be more straightforward later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Before the witness starts giving evidence, there's just a formality that we need to address. You will recall that on the 30th of March, 2007, the Prosecution filed a confidential Prosecution motion for leave to amend witness list by adding this witness as a 92 ter witness and for protective measures filed -- and for protective measures. Basically, in it the Prosecution sought the amendment of the 65 ter list to include this witness, permission for his appearance, testimony and protective measures. I wasn't here on the last session of the sitting of the 4th April, but having checked the minutes of that sitting, the motion was not opposed by the Defence, and it was granted orally by our colleague, Judge Kwon, in the course of that sitting. The only thing that remains to be done is that if you are offering him as a 92 ter witness, you haven't specifically asked for that as yet. So you asked for his inclusion in the 65 ter list, but the question of whether he's been accepted as a 92 ter witness has still not yet been decided. Do I take it that there are no objections for having this witness testify as a 92 ter witness from any of the Defence teams? I hear no objections, so he can testify as a 92 ter witness. All right. Now, good morning once more to you, Witness, and on behalf of my colleagues, Judge Kwon and Judge Prost and Judge Stole, in his absence, I would like to welcome you. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be testifying the truth. So could I kindly ask you to stand up, please, and read the text of the solemn declaration that is being handed to you now, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. The witness has a pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If Madam Usher could just provide assistance in providing the witness with what has been marked for identification as P02775.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, please take a look at this piece of paper, and then tell us whether your name is on it, without actually saying your name out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see it. Can you show it to the Defence or some of the Defence teams, anyone who wishes to see it. I thank you. That will be entered in the records as an exhibit and it will remain under seal. We'll give it a number later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall providing a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 20th of April, as well as the 26th of April of this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And was the statements at these times truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read your statement before you came here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to correct it prior to signing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: I did have the opportunity to read it, and I abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the statement that you read is true, accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions again, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I will now read a short summary of the statement: "The witness is a Bosnian Muslim. He has been a Ham radio operator since 1986 and learned how to use various types of radio communications equipment prior to his mobilisation into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "In late 1992, he was drafted into the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit attached to the 215th Brigade of the BiH Army. In early 1995, he was sent to work as an intercept operator at the northern facility, and he stayed in this location until late 1995, when he was demobilised. "The witness's work practice followed the established procedure of scanning, recording and transcribing intercepts into notebooks. Normal practice was to work in eight-hour shifts, followed by a longer break. The soldiers present were divided into two alternating groups, each of whom would be working in seven-day shift rotations. "The witness recognised his handwriting when shown the intercept dated 28 October 1995 at 11.20 hours at ERN 0078-5647 to 0078-5648, and confirms that he transcribed this intercept." This ends the summary of the statement, which, for the record, is P02777.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, sir, I just have a follow-up question for you, and that is: Have you had a chance to review the intercept in this original notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you confirm at that time that it was your original handwriting or your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Soljan. On my list, unless it has been updated, I have got three Defence teams that do not wish to cross-examine this witness, and that's the Borovcanin, Gvero and Pandurevic teams. I would like confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Confirmed on behalf of General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZEROVIC
utterances.text: Also on behalf of Borovcanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I have the Miletic Defence team will require one hour, and then the Popovic, Beara and Nikolic Defence teams. So I suggest you start, Madame Fauveau, unless there is an arrangement that someone else will. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you for some clarifications of the statement you provided to the Prosecutor on the 20th of April, 2007. In that statement, actually, the facility where you were, we refer to it as the northern location, so for specific reasons we do not mention its name, so when you are referring to the northern location, I would like you to know that that refers to the facility where you were in the course of 1995. Amongst other things, I saw in your statement that in February 1995, you attended a course which lasted 15 days, for seven to eight hours each day. My question is if the course was organised for all members of your unit or just for those who were selected from units and then sent to attend the course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: The course was organised for members. Actually, I think all members of my unit attended the course, as well as members of other units who were performing the same duties within the 2nd Corps. I think that they all -- or everyone was supposed to go through the course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the 15 days that you attended the course, did you see members of other units there and that was -- on the basis of that, you concluded that they were attending the same course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, it was a long time ago. I think that there were members of other units there. The course was organised at the level of the corps. I don't remember everyone who was there, but I think that it was attended by members of other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct if I say that you received some basic instructions at the course for intercepting communications, how to operate the equipment, and which methodology to apply in the work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, we received some basic theoretical guidance that we lacked. We received the basic training required for our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you instructed at the time on how to work, how to organise your work; in other words, that you needed to transcribe the conversations into the notebook, how to do it, how to proceed from there, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: I and a considerable number of my colleagues had already been doing that work for a couple of years, two or three years, from 1992 onwards, so that, in a sense, the operative things were something that we were already familiar with. It was a course to cover this kind of thing in a formal way. Honestly speaking, I cannot remember if the course covered the extent of our work and other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, if you remember, if not at the course, then if you can remember generally, who issued instructions for your work? Who organised work at the location where you were, within your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: There was a command structure. There were section commanders, platoon commanders. There was a command of the division while I was at that location, and then within the command there was an officer in charge of organising this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you said in your statement that the last three months at the northern location, you primarily worked on data processing, and you explained that the data processing comprised gathering information from the three work stations that were operating, then deciding which information was important, conveying or transferring this information into the computer, and then drafting short summary reports which were then forwarded to the command. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to explain what it means when you say "gathering" or "compiling" the information from the three work stations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: The operators at the work stations decided, themselves, which conversations were important and which were not. So they recorded a number of conversations, and those they considered important were transcribed, written down verbatim into the notebook. What you are asking me about now is that actually I was often the person who would take each of the notebooks and take from the notebooks what, in my opinion, was the most important thing, then I would copy that or and pass it on or send it to the command. What I mean to say is that not everything that was recorded was not transcribed, and everything that was written down in the notebooks was not sent to the command, only that which we considered important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also said that you decided which of the information was important. You just said that. But you also just said that the information was sent to the command, and I see that in the statement, that it says that you typed them into the computer. So could you please tell me if that means that you also sent the reports out or you just typed them into the computer and then someone else sent them off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: I typed them into the computer. Then I would copy that onto a diskette, and I would give the diskette to the communication centre, which was at the same facility but in the other part of the building, there was a communication centre, and they would then send that to the command. They used package radio or digital communication to -- to send the reports out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So this part of the sentence, where you say that you sent summary reports to the command, you actually mean that you typed that into the computer and copied that onto a diskette?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: On a daily basis, I would draft a report, copy it onto a diskette, and then hand that to the communication centre, which would then send that to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement, you say that you sent off summary reports. Does that mean that these were just brief reports containing the key information that you felt was important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: No. I would literally copy into the report what was written in the notebooks, but only those conversations that I felt were important. I didn't analyse the conversations. I would type them exactly the way they were written into the notebooks, but I would only do that with those conversations that I felt were important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude that your assertion that you sent summary reports is not accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Well, it depends what you mean, summary reports. "Summary" in the sense that, I repeat, we did not send out everything that we had written down. We only sent out things that we considered important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Reading this part of the statement that I put to you, I see that you put those two things differently. You said that you decided which information was important, that you typed that into the computer, and then you sent out summary reports. Now you say that these summary reports are the same as the selection of the information that would be sent out. So it arises from your statement that these are two different things. If you wish, I can show you the statement. We can look at it on the monitor, if you would like to refresh your memory. This is statement P2777 from the Prosecutor's list. It's paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, you can show that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You will see it on the screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not being broadcast? No, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I abide by what I have said before. If I have used the term "summary," it just means summary in the sense that not all the conversations that were written in the notebooks were sent out, only those that we selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, are you trying to say that the term "summary" was used by mistake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Perhaps a more appropriate term could have been used, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the same statement, paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last sentence. It reads: "The one who was responsible to write a report would take the most important facts and forward them to the command."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My impression is that this again seems to point to a summary report. Do you share my opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: No. As I have said, when we referred to what is important, we mean the conversations that are important. When I said the one who was responsible to write the report would take the most important facts, I meant that he would choose the conversations that he considered to be important. He would copy them and send them to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you yourself decide which channels you would listen in to, or did you get instructions from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: In this period of time, when we're talking about this period and this facility, we were aware of a certain number of directions and in agreement with the command -- or, rather, pursuant to instructions from the command we monitored certain directions. Since I mentioned "in agreement with," I meant there was a certain system of subordination with other units so as to avoid doubling the monitoring, so that more units would not be monitoring the same directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that -- I don't know what word you actually used, the agreement that you made with other units, does that mean that you cooperated with them in that respect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: No, we didn't cooperate. This was resolved by our command, our division command. There was an officer in charge of these affairs, and he would receive orders from the chief of this branch in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you personally aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell only you or some other people as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: I think other members of this unit knew this as well, but I can't assert that for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, your 20 minutes are soon up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am finished. I just have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will be finishing very quickly. I see that in this same statement, I don't think I need to show it to you now, that you said that you primarily monitored Banja Luka-Belgrade, the Brcko-Modrica and the Bijeljina-Krivik [phoen]-Zvornik directions. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I think it may make sense to actually point to the actual paragraph where this is, because that citation wasn't entirely as it is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness look at paragraph 13 of this statement, please? And then he can tell us what is involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at paragraph 13 of your statement, where it says that when you moved to this northern facility, you primarily monitored communications Banja Luka-Belgrade, Brcko-Modrica and Bijeljina-Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: In my statement, it says: "Banja Luka-Modrica-Brcko-Bijeljina-Belgrade and Bijeljina-Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then we must have received another statement, I apologise, a different one. Maybe the order has been changed. It is Banja Luka-Modrica-Brcko-Bijeljina-Belgrade and Bijeljina-Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We had an earlier statement which was not signed, and I was quoting from that one? And just one more point, which will bring my cross-examination to an end, or rather two. In your statement, you said that among other things, you had to note in the notebook the date, time and frequency at the beginning of every conversation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these were the instructions you received, I assume, again from your command, that that is how you should work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes, that was the instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the last point I wish to ask you about has to do with the notebooks. You said that the notebooks, when they were completed, would be handed over to the commander. You said every notebook would be handed to the commander when it was completed. So could you tell me, did you then receive a new notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you transcribe those conversations in a single notebook until it was filled; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2438B, could that document be shown to the witness, and P2438A is the English version of this transcribed intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, the conversation that you see on the screen, "Saturday, the 28th of October, 1995," is that a conversation that you transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-166
utterances.text: Yes. But you said "Sunday" and it says "Saturday" here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about that, Madame Fauveau, because in the transcript it is "Saturday."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
